name: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
info: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen is a statement of human and civil rights set by France's National Constituent Assembly in 1789, a core text of the French Revolution and a basis of later French constitutions.

facts.made: France's National Constituent Assembly, 1789; drafted first by the Marquis de Lafayette with Thomas Jefferson's assistance, with the majority of the final draft coming from Abbé Sieyès and Honoré Mirabeau's editing
facts.form: A French political and legal text of a preamble and seventeen articles, adopted as a statement of principle before a constitution
facts.where: Included at the beginning of the constitutions of the French Fourth Republic (1946) and Fifth Republic (1958) and considered valid as constitutional law; the 1789 version, the first printed one, is on UNESCO's Memory of the World International Register
facts.known: "Men are born and remain free and equal in rights"; the natural rights of liberty, property, safety and resistance to oppression; popular sovereignty; equality before the law; freedom of speech and press; the exclusion of women and the debate over active and passive citizens; its influence on the Haitian Revolution

t: The declaration set out a single set of rights held to be universal, valid at all times and in every place, and declared sovereignty to reside in the Nation rather than in a king.
Its rights belonged only to men, and the 1791 Constitution divided men into active and passive citizens, so that only about 4.3 million of some 29 million people were granted the vote.
Olympe de Gouges answered it with a declaration for women, and it inspired the uprisings of enslaved people in Saint-Domingue, though it did not mention slavery.
dyk: Olympe de Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen of 1791 follows the seventeen articles of the 1789 text point for point, and Camille Naish has described it as "almost a parody" of the original.
ev: The National Constituent Assembly adopts the last article of the declaration on 26 August, as the first step towards a constitution for the Kingdom of France
Olympe de Gouges publishes her Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen, modelled on the declaration
A second and longer declaration is written out but never formally adopted
The Convention, dominated by the Jacobins, abolishes slavery, including in Saint-Domingue and Guadeloupe
Slavery in France is finally abolished
The declaration is included at the beginning of the constitution of the Fourth Republic
The declaration is incorporated into the constitution of the Fifth Republic
UNESCO adds the 1789 version, the first printed one, to its Memory of the World International Register

sections.origins:
The declaration was set by France's National Constituent Assembly in 1789, during the French Revolution, as the first step towards writing a constitution for the Kingdom of France. Its content emerged largely from the ideals of the Enlightenment: individualism, the social contract as theorised by the Genevan philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau, and the separation of powers espoused by the Baron de Montesquieu. The American Declaration of Independence of 4 July 1776 had preceded it and drew on the same political philosophy.

These principles were widely shared throughout European society rather than confined to a small elite. Improvements in education and literacy over the 18th century meant larger audiences for newspapers and journals, and Masonic lodges, coffee houses and reading clubs provided places where people could debate ideas. The emergence of this public sphere led to Paris replacing Versailles as the cultural and intellectual centre, leaving the Court isolated and less able to influence opinion.

Lafayette, assisted by Jefferson, then the American diplomat to France, prepared a draft that echoed some provisions of the American declaration. There was no consensus on the role of the Crown, however, and until that question was settled it was impossible to create political institutions.
sections.content:
The declaration opens with a preamble that describes the fundamental characteristics of the rights, qualifying them as "natural, unalienable and sacred" and as "simple and incontestable principles" on which citizens could base their demands. Article I states that "Men are born and remain free and equal in rights. Social distinctions may be founded only upon the general good." Article II names the natural and imprescriptible rights of man as liberty, property, safety and resistance against oppression.

Article III places the principle of sovereignty in the Nation, in contrast to the divine right of kings that characterised the French monarchy. Articles IV to VI treat liberty as doing anything that does not harm others, limited only by law, and define the law as the expression of the general will, the same for all. Citizens are equally admissible to all public dignities, places and employments according to their capacity, which eliminated the special rights of the nobility and clergy.

Later articles forbid arbitrary arrest, require that penalties be established before an offence, presume innocence, protect opinions, including religious ones, and the free communication of thoughts, and require taxes to be consented to and equally distributed. Article XVI holds that a society without a guarantee of rights or a separation of powers has no constitution, and Article XVII calls property an inviolable and sacred right.
sections.making:
Lafayette prepared the principal drafts in consultation with his close friend Jefferson. The Assembly's representatives then discussed the declaration on the basis of a 24-article draft proposed by the sixth bureau, one of thirty conference groups in the Assembly, led by Jérôme Champion de Cicé, and the draft was modified during debate. In August 1789 Abbé Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès and Honoré Mirabeau played a central role in conceptualising and drafting the final text. The majority of the final draft is said to have come from Sieyès, and Mirabeau edited it before publication on 26 August as a statement of principle.

Lafayette's draft had been presented to the legislative committee on 11 July 1789 and rejected by pragmatists such as Jean Joseph Mounier, President of the Assembly, who feared creating expectations that could not be satisfied. Conservatives such as Gérard de Lally-Tollendal wanted two chambers, with an upper house appointed by the king, who would hold a veto. On 10 September the majority led by Sieyès and Talleyrand rejected this in favour of a single assembly, with Louis XVI retaining only a suspensive veto, by which he could delay a law but not block it.
sections.reception:
The final draft contained provisions then considered radical in any European society, let alone in France in 1789. The historian Georges Lefebvre argued that, combined with the elimination of privilege and feudalism, it highlighted equality in a way the American Declaration of Independence did not. The two also differed in intent. Jefferson saw the American Constitution and Bill of Rights as fixing the political system at a specific point in time, whereas the French declaration was treated as an aspirational vision and the 1791 Constitution as a starting point. The declaration was not deeply rooted in the practice of the West or even of France at the time, and it met opposition, since democracy and individual rights were often regarded as synonymous with anarchy and subversion.

Its rights were awarded only to men. The 1791 Constitution distinguished between active citizens, who were French men at least 25 years old who paid taxes equal to three days' work and were not servants, and passive citizens. The vote went to approximately 4.3 million Frenchmen out of a population of around 29 million, and the omitted groups included women, the poor, domestic servants, enslaved people, children and foreigners. For this reason the Constitution was never fully accepted by radicals in the Jacobin club.
sections.survival:
The declaration survived as a text that later constitutions took up rather than replaced. It was attached as a preamble to the French Constitution of 1791 and to that of the Third Republic, which lasted from 1870 to 1940, and it was incorporated into the current Constitution of France in 1958. It is also included at the beginning of the constitutions of the Fourth Republic (1946) and Fifth Republic (1958) and is considered valid as constitutional law.

A second and longer declaration, also known as the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen of 1793, was written out in 1793 but never formally adopted. The legislation on active citizens, passed in 1789, was amended by the creators of the Constitution of the Year III to remove the label of active citizen, but the power to vote was then granted solely to substantial property owners.

In 2003 UNESCO added the 1789 version of the declaration, the first printed version, to its Memory of the World International Register, recognising it as documentary heritage of global importance.
sections.legacy:
The declaration had a significant impact on the development of popular conceptions of individual liberty and democracy in Europe and worldwide. It became the basis for a nation of free individuals protected equally by the law, and it embodies ideals and aspirations towards which France pledged to struggle in the future.

Its limits drew challenges in its own time. After the Women's March on Versailles on 5 October 1789, women presented a petition to the National Assembly proposing a decree giving women equal rights, and in 1790 Nicolas de Condorcet and Etta Palm d'Aelders unsuccessfully called on the Assembly to extend civil and political rights to women. Olympe de Gouges then published her declaration in September 1791, which exposed what she saw as the failure of a revolution devoted to equality.

The declaration did not revoke slavery in the French colonies, which Jacques-Pierre Brissot's Les Amis des Noirs lobbied for and the planters of the Club Massiac opposed. It did not mention slavery, yet it inspired the uprisings in Saint-Domingue in the Haitian Revolution, as C. L. R. James discusses in The Black Jacobins, and the organisers of the Pointe Coupée Slave Conspiracy of 1795 in Louisiana also drew on it. The French Penal Code of 1791 did not mention sodomy as a crime, so that no one could be prosecuted for it, a situation the personal freedom given by the document is held to have created.

summary: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was set by France's National Constituent Assembly in 1789. It declared liberty, equality before the law and popular sovereignty, though for men only, and it still stands at the head of France's constitution.
references: William Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution (Oxford University Press, 1989)
Georges Lefebvre, The French Revolution: From Its Origins to 1793 (Columbia University Press, 1962)
Simon Schama, Citizens: A Chronicle of the French Revolution (Penguin, 1989)
notes: The article credits the drafting to Lafayette (with Jefferson), to Sieyès (the majority of the final draft) and to Mirabeau (a central role, and the editing); the text reports each as stated and does not rank them.
The article says the Assembly worked from a 24-article draft of the sixth bureau and does not say how it became seventeen articles; the facts line says seventeen because the article lists seventeen.
The article says the last article was adopted on 26 August 1789 and also that Mirabeau's edited text was 'published on 26 August'; both are used as given.
Lefebvre's comparison and the article's claim that Jefferson saw the American texts as fixing the system are attributed in the text.
The article gives the Constitution of the Year III as amending the 1789 active-citizen legislation, without a date; none was added.

The survival section says nothing of manuscripts: the article names none. The 1946 and 1958 inclusion is stated twice in different wording in the article; the 1791 Constitution and the Third Republic are given as preamble.
Left out as beyond the article's measure: the 1793 declaration's content, the 'Declaration of Franchimont' and other early declarations in the See also list.
